subject: arvr
title: Unit 3 MCQs — Augmented and Virtual Reality

items.q: What is Augmented Reality?
options: A computer-generated simulation of a three-dimensional environment
The integration of digital information with the user's real-world environment in real time
A fully immersive experience in a computer-generated environment
The use of virtual elements without any connection to the real world
items.explain: AR **enhances** the real world by overlaying digital content **in real time**, and the user **remains connected to reality**. Options (a) and (c) describe **VR**; (d) describes neither.

items.q: Which is **NOT** one of the three requirements an AR system must satisfy?
options: Combines real and virtual
Interactive in real time
Registered in 3D
Displayed on a head-mounted display
items.explain: AR is defined by the **three requirements**, not by hardware — phones, tablets and projectors all qualify, and **audio AR** satisfies the definition with no display at all. A CGI film fails *interactive*; a HUD fails *registered in 3D*.

items.q: Why is registration harder in AR than in VR?
options: AR displays have lower resolution
The user sees the real world and virtual content simultaneously, so any misalignment is directly visible
AR runs at lower frame rates
AR cannot use quaternions
items.explain: In VR a tracking error shifts the **whole world together** and often goes unnoticed. In AR the virtual object **visibly slides off** the real surface it should sit on. AR has no error budget VR lacks — it just has **nowhere to hide**.

items.q: The 'Sword of Damocles' (1968) is significant because it was:
options: The first outdoor AR system
The first head-mounted display, overlaying wireframe graphics on the real world
The first system to use natural feature tracking
The first collaborative AR system
items.explain: Ivan Sutherland's HMD — so heavy it hung from the ceiling. It is simultaneously the **first AR and first VR system**, since the distinction did not yet exist.

items.q: What made Vuforia (2008) a turning point for AR?
options: It was the first AR system to use GPS
It enabled natural feature tracking on smartphones, removing the need to prepare the environment
It introduced the first AR head-mounted display
It was the first collaborative AR platform
items.explain: Before this, AR needed **fiducial markers** placed in the scene. Natural feature tracking works on **ordinary images and objects**, which is the difference between a lab demo and something shippable to a million phones.

items.q: Which AR application example is associated with **IKEA Place**?
options: Industrial assembly guidance
Surgical navigation
Previewing furniture in your own space before buying
Outdoor navigation overlays
items.explain: **Retail** — customers assess **size, colour and style** before purchasing, improving engagement and **reducing product returns**. The value depends entirely on **correct scale**, i.e. good registration.

items.q: A 360° video that the user can look around but cannot influence is an example of:
options: A closed-loop interactive system
An open-loop non-interactive system
Augmented virtuality
A spatial projection system
items.explain: **Open loop** — there is **no feedback path**; turning your head changes what you look at but not what the system does. **Closed-loop** systems modify the environment in response to user actions, and that is what makes it VR rather than cinema.

items.q: The **uncanny valley** describes:
options: The gap between virtual and real object positions
The drop in affinity when a virtual character is almost — but not quite — human-like
The dead zone in a tracking system's working volume
The mismatch between vergence and accommodation
items.explain: Affinity rises with human likeness, then **collapses just short of realism** because small imperfections read as *wrong*. The practical lesson: a **stylised avatar is often more comfortable than a nearly-photoreal one**.

items.q: **Presence** in VR is best described as:
options: The frame rate at which the display runs
The psychological sensation of 'being there' in the virtual environment
The number of tracked degrees of freedom
The physical space available for room-scale movement
items.explain: Presence is **psychological**, not technical — which is why it cannot be bought with resolution alone. The test is behavioural: does the user **duck** or **flinch**? The **Birdly** simulator achieves it by adding wind and motion, not pixels.

items.q: A VR experience built from 360° video or photogrammetry of a real location is a:
options: Synthetic world
Captured world
Augmented virtuality
Open-loop projection
items.explain: **Captured worlds** are reconstructions of real places — photorealistic by construction but often limited in interactivity (360° video has no geometry to interact with). **Synthetic worlds** are entirely computer-generated, offering limitless creativity but requiring everything to be modelled.

items.q: **Clouds Over Sidra** is cited as an example of VR used for:
options: Surgical training
Empathy-building in humanitarian work
Architectural walkthroughs
Rhythm-based gaming
items.explain: It places users in the life of a **12-year-old Syrian refugee**. It works because **presence** makes the experience emotionally different from watching a documentary — the strongest practical evidence that presence is real.

items.q: How are **Video See-Through** displays in AR distinctively characterized?
options: By strategically placing projectors for spatial projections
By presenting captured images on head-mounted displays
By utilizing transparent displays for virtual object augmentation
By projecting virtual objects onto the physical world
items.explain: VST uses **cameras to capture the real world**, composites virtual content with it, and shows the result on **internal screens**. Option (c) describes **OST**; (a) and (d) describe **spatial projection**.

items.q: Which is a fundamental limitation of **optical see-through** displays?
options: They add latency to the real-world view
Virtual content is additive only, so it cannot occlude the real world
They cannot be used outdoors
They require external base stations
items.explain: An optical combiner **adds** light and cannot subtract it, so true black is impossible and holograms look **ghostly** — you always see the wall through them. Latency in the real-world view is a **VST** problem; OST is zero-latency because you see reality **directly**.

items.q: What is the primary distinction between **world-fixed** and **user-fixed** displays?
options: World-fixed displays are stationary, while user-fixed displays dynamically adjust based on the user's movements
World-fixed displays are external screens, while user-fixed displays are integrated into eyewear
World-fixed displays follow the user's viewpoint, while user-fixed displays remain fixed in the physical environment
World-fixed displays support only 2D projections, while user-fixed displays offer 3D holographic projections
items.explain: **World-fixed content is anchored to the environment** and demands full 6DOF registration; **user-fixed content moves with the user** and needs little world tracking. Option (c) reverses the definitions — the classic distractor.

items.q: A CAVE system is an example of:
options: An optical see-through HMD
A video see-through HMD
A spatial projection system
An inside-out tracking system
items.explain: **CAVE (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment)** projects visuals onto the walls and floor of a room-sized cube — **no headset needed**, naturally multi-user, but a **fixed, expensive installation** correct from only one tracked viewpoint.

items.q: How does **Differential GPS (D-GPS)** improve a user's position estimate?
options: It relies on satellites measuring atmospheric distortions
It uses a correction signal from ground stations to compensate for atmospheric distortions
It uses an outside-in system with signals transmitted from Earth to satellites
The accuracy of GPS is fixed and does not vary with measurement conditions
items.explain: A **ground station at a precisely known location** derives the current error (mostly atmospheric) and **broadcasts a correction** to nearby receivers, improving accuracy from metres to **sub-metre**. (c) reverses the signal direction; (d) is simply false.

items.q: What is the difference between **outside-in** and **inside-out** tracking?
options: Outside-in uses cameras on the headset; inside-out uses external base stations
Outside-in uses fixed external sensors watching the headset; inside-out uses the headset's own cameras watching the room
Outside-in works only outdoors; inside-out works only indoors
Outside-in is 3DOF; inside-out is 6DOF
items.explain: **Outside-in** (Lighthouse, camera rigs) is very accurate and low-drift because the reference is genuinely fixed — but needs installation. **Inside-out** (Quest, HoloLens) is portable with no setup, but the headset must build its own map — **SLAM**.

items.q: What is the primary function of a **Virtual World Generator** in a VR system?
options: To create physical objects within the virtual environment
To process user inputs and commands for VR interactions
To manage the state and behaviour of virtual objects and simulate environmental physics
To convert 3D models into 2D images for the display
items.explain: The VWG is the **core application layer** owning **state, physics and interaction coordination**. Option (d) is the **rendering engine**; (b) is the **input processing system**.

items.q: Why does a VR rendering engine target **60–120 fps**?
options: To match the refresh rate of desktop monitors
To minimise latency and prevent motion sickness
Because stereoscopic rendering cannot run slower
To reduce GPU power consumption
items.explain: The frame rate exists to keep **motion-to-photon latency** low enough that vision and the vestibular sense agree. Note that a **consistent** rate matters more than a high one — oscillating frame rate is itself a sickness trigger.

items.q: **Stereoscopic rendering** means:
options: Rendering at twice the resolution
Generating separate images for each eye to produce depth
Using two GPUs in parallel
Rendering the scene twice for anti-aliasing
items.explain: Two view matrices offset by the user's **inter-pupillary distance**, two viewports, two projection matrices — the whole Unit 2 pipeline **run twice per frame**. This is why the VR polygon budget is roughly half a monitor's.

items.q: Which eye movement is essential for maintaining a stable visual field and is particularly relevant to VR hardware design for preventing motion sickness?
options: Saccades
Microsaccades
Optokinetic reflex
Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex
items.explain: The **VOR** counter-rotates the eyes against head motion with **~10 ms latency**, and is calibrated to a perfectly stable real world. If the display lags, the eyes compensate correctly but the image hasn't updated — the world **slips across the retina**, producing sensory conflict and sickness.

items.q: Roughly how much of the visual field does the **fovea** cover, and why does it matter for VR?
options: About 2°, enabling foveated rendering
About 20°, enabling wide field-of-view displays
About 90°, matching headset optics
The entire field, which is why resolution must be uniform
items.explain: High-acuity vision covers only ~2° of a ~200° field — you see almost nothing sharply. **Foveated rendering** exploits this: full resolution near the gaze point, lower resolution outside, saving **50–70%** of shading cost with eye tracking.

items.q: What is the **vergence–accommodation conflict**?
options: The eyes converge on a virtual object at one depth while the lens must focus at the display's fixed distance
The mismatch between head rotation and eye rotation
The conflict between visual and vestibular motion cues
The difference in image between the left and right eye
items.explain: In the real world **vergence and accommodation change together**; in a headset vergence varies with virtual depth while focus is fixed at the screen's optical distance. Result: **eye strain and fatigue** — the deepest unsolved problem in headset design. Option (c) is sensory conflict causing motion sickness, a different problem.

items.q: Why do VR headsets use **low-persistence** displays?
options: To save power
Because while the eye smoothly pursues a moving object, a sample-and-hold image smears across the retina
To increase perceived brightness
To reduce the vergence–accommodation conflict
items.explain: Illuminating each frame for only **1–2 ms** gives the eye no time to smear it — the same reason a fast camera shutter freezes motion. Counter-intuitively, the fix for blur is to show the image **less**.

items.q: During a **saccade**, vision is largely suppressed. Which VR technique exploits this?
options: Stereoscopic rendering
Redirected walking — subtly rotating the virtual world mid-saccade
Low-persistence display timing
Inter-pupillary distance adjustment
items.explain: **Saccadic suppression** means the user cannot perceive changes made during the jump, so the system can rotate the world imperceptibly — letting them walk in circles in a small room while believing they walk straight.

items.q: What are the **six degrees of freedom** of a tracked rigid body?
options: Six rotation axes
Three translations (surge, sway, heave) and three rotations (roll, pitch, yaw)
Three positions and three velocities
Two for each of x, y and z
items.explain: **3 translation + 3 rotation.** A 3DOF device (Google Cardboard) gives orientation only — you can look around but leaning forward brings you no closer to anything.

items.q: How is the **pose** of a tracked rigid body best represented mathematically?
options: Three Euler angles
A position vector $\mathbf p \in \mathbb{R}^3$ together with a unit quaternion $q$
A 3×3 rotation matrix only
A single scalar distance from the origin
items.explain: **$(\mathbf p, q)$** — position plus a **unit quaternion**, chosen over Euler angles because it avoids gimbal lock and interpolates smoothly. Equivalently a $4\times4$ homogeneous matrix, which is the object's frame in world coordinates.

items.q: A tracker reports a pose that is correct on average but varies by 2 mm when nothing is moving. This is a problem of:
options: Poor accuracy
Poor precision (jitter)
High latency
Drift
items.explain: Right on average = **good accuracy**; varying reading = **poor precision**. This is the more objectionable failure — humans are far more sensitive to **motion** than to a constant offset, so jitter makes content visibly shake.

items.q: Which tracking technology requires **no line of sight** between sensor and transmitter?
options: Optical marker-based
Ultrasonic
Electromagnetic
Mechanical
items.explain: **EM tracking** measures magnetic field strength and can track **through obstructions** — which is why it survives in **surgical navigation**, where the instrument tip is inside the patient. Its weakness is **metal and electronic interference**.

items.q: **Polhemus** systems are the named example of which tracking technology?
options: Mechanical
Electromagnetic
Ultrasonic
Optical
items.explain: **Polhemus** is the classic electromagnetic tracker, widely used in VR and motion capture. **ARToolKit** is the optical marker-based example; medical simulators exemplify mechanical.

items.q: Why do ultrasonic trackers have slow update rates?
options: Their processors are slow
Sound travels at ~343 m/s, so a few metres of round trip costs milliseconds before any computation
They require a magnetic field to stabilise
They can only sample once per frame
items.explain: A 3 m round trip takes ~9 ms **purely in flight** — most of a 20 ms latency budget. **Reflections** compound it, since an echo is indistinguishable from a farther object.

items.q: What distinguishes **marker-based** from **markerless (natural feature)** tracking?
options: Marker-based uses cameras; markerless uses magnetic fields
Marker-based relies on fiducial patterns placed in the scene; markerless tracks natural features like corners and textures
Marker-based is markerless with more markers
Marker-based works outdoors only
items.explain: Markers are **guaranteed, high-contrast targets of known geometry** — easy to solve, but someone must place them. Natural features are **already everywhere** but must be found, matched and tracked, and can **drift**. Markers moved AR out of the lab; markerless moved it out of prepared environments.

items.q: Why does a gyroscope's orientation estimate **drift**?
options: Because it measures acceleration rather than rotation
Because a constant bias in angular velocity integrates into an error growing linearly with time
Because magnetic fields distort its reading
Because it only samples at 30 Hz
items.explain: A gyro reports **angular velocity**, so orientation requires **integration**. A bias $\epsilon$ becomes an error $\epsilon t$ — a bias of 0.01°/s reaches **36° after an hour**. Fast and smooth short-term; useless long-term.

items.q: Why is inertial **position** tracking from an accelerometer alone impossible?
options: Accelerometers cannot measure motion
Position needs double integration, so a bias produces error growing quadratically with time
Accelerometers only work when stationary
Accelerometers measure only vertical acceleration
items.explain: Error $\propto \tfrac12\epsilon t^2$ — a bias of 0.01 m/s² gives **18 cm of error after 6 seconds**. This is exactly why 6DOF headsets need cameras or base stations, and why 3DOF devices are cheap.

items.q: What is the accelerometer's actual role in orientation tracking?
options: Computing position by double integration
Providing an absolute reference for roll and pitch by measuring gravity
Providing absolute heading
Measuring angular velocity
items.explain: It measures **gravity**, giving an absolute **vertical** reference — hence roll and pitch. It **cannot give yaw**, because rotating about the vertical axis doesn't change how gravity feels; that requires a **magnetometer**.

items.q: In 3D orientation tracking using quaternions, how is the final orientation computed recursively from a series of delta quaternions?
options: By subtracting each delta quaternion from the final quaternion
By multiplying each delta quaternion with the running quaternion
By adding the delta quaternions to the final quaternion
By dividing the final quaternion by each delta quaternion
items.explain: Quaternions **compose by multiplication**, like rotation matrices — that is what composing rotations means. Adding two unit quaternions does not even give a unit quaternion. Order encodes the frame: $q\otimes\Delta q$ is body-frame, $\Delta q\otimes q$ is global.

items.q: 1D gyroscope readings over 10 seconds are 8.01, 0.27, 5.04, 5.85, 3.06, 4.05, 2.88, 8.28, 4.59, 2.97 °/s. With the body initially at $(1,0)$ and a 1-second time step, what is the final position?
items.explain: With $\Delta t = 1$ s the total rotation is just the **sum** = **45.0°**. Rotating $(1,0)$ by 45° gives $(\cos 45°, \sin 45°) = (0.707, 0.707)$. Note $(1.414, 1.414)$ is wrong because **rotation preserves length** — the point must stay at radius 1.

items.q: Given a gyroscope reading $\boldsymbol\omega = (5.73, 11.46, 17.19)$ °/s, what is the **axis** of rotation?
items.explain: The axis is the **normalised** angular-velocity vector: $\lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert = 21.44$, so $\hat{\mathbf u} = (5.73, 11.46, 17.19)/21.44 = (0.267, 0.535, 0.802)$. Note the components are in the ratio $1:2:3$ — a useful sanity check.

items.q: Why is **position** tracking fundamentally harder than **orientation** tracking?
options: Position needs more sensors
Orientation has cheap absolute references (gravity, magnetic north) while position has none
Position changes faster than orientation
Quaternions cannot represent position
items.explain: Nothing you can *feel* tells you where you are. Orientation is recoverable from a £2 IMU; position requires an **external reference** — cameras, base stations or GPS. This asymmetry is why 3DOF headsets are cheap and 6DOF ones need cameras.

items.q: In tracking attached bodies, what does **inverse kinematics** compute?
options: The end-effector position, given the joint angles
The joint angles, given a desired end-effector pose
The mass of each link
The velocity of the root body
items.explain: **IK: position → angles** (may have many solutions or none). **FK: angles → position** (straightforward concatenation). VR avatar animation is an **IK** problem — the headset knows only head and two hands and must solve for plausible elbows.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes **drift** from **noise**?
options: Drift is random and fixed by filtering; noise is systematic and fixed by fusion
Drift is systematic and accumulates, needing an absolute reference; noise is random and is reduced by filtering
Both are random and both are fixed by averaging
Drift affects only position; noise affects only orientation
items.explain: **You cannot filter away drift and you cannot fuse away noise.** Averaging a biased sensor gives you the bias; drift needs something that **knows the truth** (gravity, north, a camera). Noise is zero-mean and **does** average out.

items.q: A **complementary filter** combines gyroscope and accelerometer data by:
options: Averaging the two equally
High-passing the gyroscope and low-passing the accelerometer
Using the gyroscope indoors and the accelerometer outdoors
Discarding whichever reading is larger
items.explain: $\theta_{k+1} = \alpha(\theta_k + \omega\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{\text{accel}}$ with $\alpha \approx 0.98$. Each sensor is used only where it is good: the gyro's fast response passes, its slow drift is filtered out; the accelerometer's stable average passes, its jitter is filtered out.

items.q: Which sensor corrects **heading (yaw) drift**?
options: Accelerometer
Magnetometer
Gyroscope
Barometer
items.explain: Only the **magnetometer** gives an absolute horizontal reference (magnetic north). The **accelerometer corrects tilt drift** (roll and pitch, from gravity) but **cannot touch yaw** — rotating about vertical doesn't change how gravity feels.

items.q: Why is drift correction applied as a **small fraction** each step rather than snapping fully to the reference?
options: To save computation
Because the accelerometer is only a valid vertical reference when the device is not accelerating
Because the gyroscope updates too slowly
To preserve the quaternion's unit length
items.explain: During real motion the accelerometer measures gravity **plus** movement and is briefly wrong. Correcting slowly means the accelerometer wins over **minutes** (where the gyro drifts) and the gyro wins over **milliseconds** (where the accelerometer lies).

items.q: What is the correct order of the four sensor-fusion steps?
options: Derive roll/pitch/yaw → normalize → re-normalize → combine with gyro
Normalize accelerometer and magnetometer → derive roll/pitch/yaw → convert to quaternions and combine with gyro deltas → re-normalize
Combine with gyro deltas → normalize → derive roll/pitch/yaw → re-normalize
Normalize → re-normalize → derive roll/pitch/yaw → combine with gyro
items.explain: **① Normalize** (remove scale differences, keep direction) → **② derive Euler angles** (absolute reference) → **③ convert to quaternions and combine with gyro $\Delta q$** (fast response + long-term stability) → **④ re-normalize** (prevent floating-point error accumulating).

items.q: Why must quaternions be **re-normalized** during sensor fusion?
options: To convert them into Euler angles
Because floating-point error and integration drift push the norm away from 1, so the 'rotation' begins to scale as well as rotate
To increase the update rate
Because the magnetometer requires unit vectors
items.explain: Only **unit** quaternions represent pure rotations. Repeated multiplication accumulates error; without periodic $q \leftarrow q/\lVert q\rVert$ small errors grow into visible misalignment of the viewpoint.

items.q: In sensor fusion, which sensor provides **fast, high-frequency** orientation data and which provides **long-term stability**?
options: Accelerometer is fast; gyroscope is stable
Gyroscope is fast; accelerometer and magnetometer provide stability
Magnetometer is fast; GPS is stable
All three are equally fast and stable
items.explain: The **gyroscope** is precise moment-to-moment but **drifts**; the **accelerometer and magnetometer** are jittery but **never drift**, because they measure things that don't move — gravity and magnetic north. Their failure modes are opposites, which is the whole trick.

items.q: A drone uses gyroscope and accelerometer for rapid adjustments, GPS for long-term positioning and a magnetometer for heading. This illustrates:
options: That drones need more sensors than headsets
The same fusion architecture as a VR headset — a fast-but-drifting sensor corrected by a slow-but-absolute one
That GPS is more accurate than an IMU
That magnetometers are the primary navigation sensor
items.explain: Swap GPS for a camera doing SLAM and you have a Quest headset. **Fusion is one idea applied wherever fast and absolute cannot come from the same sensor.**
